# The Last Watch of the Mara Celeste

---

The first tea I brought her was oolong because that's what she drank nights. I keep a tin of it separate from the breakfast blacks, up in the cabinet above the range where the damp doesn't get to it so fast. I brewed it strong the way she took it — no sugar, no milk, steep it until it's the color of varnish — and I carried it up to the bridge in the white mug, the one with the chip on the rim that she liked because it fit her hand. This was maybe ten o'clock on the first night. The wind had been building since suppertime but it hadn't got bad yet, just the long rolls that make the pots swing on their hooks and the water in the sink slosh back and forth like it's deciding something.

She was standing at the chart table with both hands flat on it, leaning her weight forward, the way you lean on a counter when your back hurts and you don't want anyone to know. She didn't look up when I came in. I set the mug on the table next to the dividers and the pencil she'd been using and I said something — I don't remember what, probably nothing worth remembering, probably "here" or "it's hot" or the kind of thing you say to someone when the thing you're really saying is *I see you standing there and I brought you this*.

She said thank you. Or she nodded. One or the other.

I went back down and scrubbed the stockpot from dinner because it had a ring of dried lentil on the inside that would set like cement if I left it. That took a while. Then I wiped down the galley counter and checked the tie-downs on the dry stores because the rolls were getting longer and I didn't want to chase cans across the floor at two in the morning. By the time I went back up — to collect the mug, that's all, just to collect it and wash it because I don't leave mugs sitting — the tea was cold. I could tell without touching it. The surface had that flat look, no steam, and it trembled with the engine vibration in a way that hot liquid doesn't. Hot liquid moves from within. Cold liquid just receives whatever the world does to it.

She was in the same position. Both hands. Leaning.

I took the mug and went down and poured it out and rinsed it and filled the kettle again. I don't know what time it was then. The clock in the galley had been wrong for weeks, gaining about ten minutes a day, and I'd stopped trusting it. I brewed the tea the same way. Strong, no sugar, steeped until it turned. I brought it back up and set it in the same spot, near enough to her right hand that she could reach it without shifting her weight, and I took the pencil she'd dropped on the floor and put it back on the table and I went down.

That one went cold too. I found it later. I poured it out. I did not make a third.

No. That's wrong. I did make a third. I made a third and I drank it myself, standing at the galley sink, because the tea was there and it was brewed and someone ought to drink it. It tasted the way her tea always tasted, which was too strong for me. I drank it all.

---

The letters I knew about because I was the one who walked to the port offices. Every harbor, every stop — Singapore, Colombo, Mombasa, wherever we tied up long enough for the mail to catch us — I'd go because I liked the walk and because the captain had things to do that were more important than fetching envelopes and because, if I'm honest, I liked being the one to bring her things. Letters, tea, the Tuesday cards, whatever small cargo I could carry that would put me in the doorway of wherever she was.

The bank letters were different from the others. Same size, more or less, cream-colored envelopes, but they had that look that official things have, the typed address with the name too formal, the stamps too neat. She got the first one in Mombasa, or maybe Dar es Salaam — I'm mixing ports now, this was months before the storm, and the ports have run together the way ports do. She read it at the chart table the way she read everything, standing, holding it close because she was vain about her eyes and wouldn't wear glasses. She didn't say anything. I was there because I'd brought coffee — mornings were coffee, Ethiopian if I could find it, though I usually couldn't and settled for whatever was cheapest at the chandler's — and she read the letter and folded it and set it down and drank the coffee and the morning went on.

The second letter she read in the galley. I don't know why she came down to read it there instead of on the bridge. Maybe she did it without thinking Probably she wanted to be where she wouldn't have to hold her face right for whoever might be watching on deck. She read it sitting on the stool near the cutting board, and when she finished she folded it — not in half, not the way you'd fold a letter to put it back, but in a series of small deliberate creases, triangles and tucks. She made a boat out of it. A paper boat, the kind children make in school, with a pointed bow and an open hull. She set it in the galley sink, which had an inch of water in it because the drain was slow, and the little boat sat there on the dirty water and turned slowly in place. She said something like *there's your fleet*. Or maybe she said *that's that*. Something short. Then she went out.

I left the paper boat in the sink longer than I should have. It softened and listed to one side and eventually the ink from the letterhead bled into the water and the water turned faintly blue. I fished it out and put it in the waste bin and scrubbed the sink with the rough side of the sponge.

After that the letters kept coming and she kept reading them and I stopped being the only one who knew. Kumar heard something — overheard a radio call, or one of the agents in port told him, the way people tell things to third parties when they want the principal to know without having to say it to her face. What I heard, what everyone heard eventually, was that the bank had sent men to Bermuda to be there when we arrived. To meet us on the dock. To take the ship.

I don't know the right word for it. Repossession, seizure, something legal that means they come with papers and the papers mean the thing that's yours isn't yours anymore. I don't know how a bank can take a ship. I don't know what a ship is, to a bank — a number, I suppose, an entry in a book that's either black or red, and hers had gone red. What I know is that after the letters started she stopped talking about the routes ahead and started talking about the routes behind, about the places the Mara Celeste had been before her, when her grandfather had it. The South China Sea in the '60s. The Cape run. The ice trade out of Norway when the ship was young and the grandfather was young and neither of them had any debt to speak of.

The grandfather's photograph was in the wheelhouse, screwed to the bulkhead above the radio where you couldn't help but see it every time you adjusted the dial. It was black and white and it had gone yellow and the glass in the frame had a crack running corner to corner that someone had taped over with electrician's tape. He looked like her. Or she looked like him — the jaw, the forehead, the way they stood with their weight pitched forward as if the ground might move and they intended to be ready. He was standing on a deck, I think, though the background had faded to a general brightness that could have been water or sky or a painted wall. She never told me much about him. She told me once that he sang in the mornings, that he knew the name of every seabird he saw, that when he died the deck of the Mara Celeste still smelled like the cardamom he used to keep in his coat pocket. That was more than she told most people. That was all she told me.

The thing I want to say about the letters is this: after they started — after the third one, maybe, or the fourth — her face changed. Not the way you'd think. Not tight, not drawn, not the face of a woman being ruined. She looked easier. She looked the way people look when they put down something they've been carrying for a long time. Her shoulders dropped. She slept longer. One morning I came up with her coffee and she was sitting in the captain's chair with her boots off and her feet on the console and she looked ten years younger than she had in Mombasa. I didn't understand it then. I think I understand it now, or I understand part of it, the part I can reach. The letters had decided something for her. She'd been trying to save the ship for years — taking bad cargo, running lean, skipping the repairs that should have happened in dry dock — and the letters told her the saving was over. There was nothing left to try. And for some people that's not a door closing. It's the end of having to stand in the doorway.

She was relieved. That's the word, and I mean it in the oldest way — relieved of duty. The bank had removed the burden of hope, and what was left underneath the hope was something quieter and more dangerous, and I didn't have a name for it then, though I have been thinking about it since, in the years since, and the closest I can get is that she had decided to keep the one promise she could still keep.

---

The third morning was bad. I knew it was bad when the mop I'd wedged against the galley door fell down for the fourth time and I stopped picking it up. The rolls had gone past the swinging stage — they were sharp now, sudden, the kind that makes you walk with your hip permanently braced against the nearest wall. I'd poured the breakfast porridge into two bowls and covered them with plates to keep them from sloshing and I carried them up one at a time. Wen was on the bridge. Most of the others were gone by then — they'd gone with Kumar on the life raft twelve hours before, maybe more, maybe less, time was already getting unreliable — and the ship felt the way a house feels when guests leave, that particular quality of air that has recently had more people in it than it does now.

I set the bowls on the chart table. She looked at them and then at me and she said *cribbage*.

I went down and got the cards.

We'd been playing since — I don't know. Since before Mombasa. Since she found out I knew how and said good, because Kumar played too slow and Davi cheated. We played mornings before the day started, sitting across from each other at the chart table or sometimes at the galley counter if the weather was fine and she came down. I kept the peg board in a drawer under the radio with a rubber band around it and the cards in a tin that used to hold throat lozenges. I brought everything up and set it on the table and the ship rolled hard to starboard and the pencil slid off and I caught it. She was already shuffling.

It was hard to play. The cards were damp — everything was damp, the air was water, you could feel moisture on your face from the spray coming in through the seals around the bridge windows — and they stuck to each other and to the table and to our fingers. I dealt. She cut. I turned up a five for the crib and she said *typical*, which was what she said when the cut didn't favor her, which was what she said roughly half the time. I sorted my hand. A six, two sevens, a nine, a queen, and I think a three. I kept the six-seven-seven-nine and put the queen and three in the crib, which was hers, which I regretted, because the three might pair something. She studied her hand longer than she needed to. She always studied her hand longer than she needed to. I'd told her a hundred times that cribbage isn't chess, the cards are the cards, you play them or you don't, and she'd told me a hundred times to stop telling her how to play.

We played. I led the six. She played a nine — fifteen for two, she said, moving her peg. I played a seven. She played something, I don't remember, a low card. We counted. She pegged. The ship rolled and the board slid and I caught it with my elbow. Neither of us mentioned the wind. You could hear it — you could feel it in your molars, the way you feel a sound that isn't really a sound anymore, more like the air itself being angry — but we didn't mention it the way you don't mention the weather when the weather is just the condition you live in.

She won. She won by eleven points, which was not close, and I told her she'd been dealt a hand that a child could win with, and she said she'd been dealt a hand that required skill, and I said *skill*, and she said *you heard me*.

I wrote the score on the pad. The pad was damp. The pencil tore through the paper a little. I wrote her name at the top the way I always did — just the W, nicked and leaning — and the number, and I underlined it, and I put the pencil down.

She ate three bites of the porridge. Cold by then, but she ate them. I watched her eat them the way I watched her eat everything, counting and measuring without meaning to, the way you do when someone's health is your responsibility. Three bites was not enough. Three bites was more than she'd eaten the day before.

I collected the bowls and the cards and the peg board and I went down. Halfway down the companion ladder I stopped because I realized I had not said any of the things I might have said, and then I went the rest of the way down because I also realized I was never going to say them, because they weren't the kind of things that go into words, not our words anyway, not the words we had built between us over however many months it had been. Our words were *cribbage* and *typical* and *the tea's hot* and *you were dealt a hand a child could win with*. That was the language. It doesn't translate into anything else. You either lived inside it or you didn't.

I washed the bowls.

---

The pumps quit sometime after the card game. I know that. I know that time moved in that direction — cards first, then the pumps — because I'd just finished scrubbing the porridge pot when the sound changed. The pumps had been running so long they'd become part of the ship's body, the way your heartbeat is part of your body, and when they stopped the silence was physical, a new pressure against the inside of your ears. Then there was water where water should not have been, and it was coming faster than it had been, and I could feel the ship sitting lower in the way you feel an elevator descend — not the motion itself but the heaviness, the commitment to down.

I went up to the bridge. Wen had moved. She was no longer at the chart table. She was at the wheel, though the wheel was doing nothing useful by then — the rudder was either gone or jammed, I never found out which. She had a length of line in her hands. Three-strand manila, a half-inch, the kind we used for lashing cargo on deck. I'd seen it coiled by the binnacle stand for days and assumed it was left over from some task. It was not left over.

She was making a loop around her waist. She pulled the line through, wrapped it once around the king spoke of the wheel, brought it back, and knotted it. A bowline. I know that much seamanship. A bowline is a loop that doesn't slip — the more you pull, the tighter it holds, but it doesn't crush. It's the knot you use when you need to trust something with your weight. She tied it the way she did everything with her hands, which was quickly and without looking down, the way people do things they've practiced so many times the knowledge lives in the fingers and not in the head.

She wrapped the line around twice more — waist, wheel, waist, wheel — and each time she tied it off with the same knot. She tested each one by leaning back and letting the rope take her weight, the way a climber tests a harness. It held. She adjusted the last loop where it sat against her hip, pushing it down so it wouldn't ride up when the angle changed.

I stood in the doorway to the bridge and I watched her hands. I should tell you what else I was looking at — the sea, the sky, the angle of the deck — but I wasn't looking at anything else. I was looking at her fingers working the line through the loop, the way the wrist turned to set the knot, the small tug she gave at the end to snug it down. Her knuckles were raw. The skin across the backs of her hands was red and cracked from the wet and the salt and the cold. Her nails were short because she kept them short, because long nails catch in things on a ship, and one of them — the thumbnail on her left hand — was blue-black underneath
